analysis.one_liner: Bars the President, cabinet officials, Members of Congress, and their immediate families from holding foreign financial interests or taking foreign payments.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred the President, cabinet officials, Members of Congress, and their families from holding foreign financial interests or taking foreign payments, was referred to two committees in September 2021 and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The Stop Foreign Payoffs Act would amend the Ethics in Government Act to prohibit the President, Members of Congress, and cabinet-level officials from holding any financial interest in a foreign business or receiving any payment from one. The same rules would apply to their spouses, children, sons-in-law, and daughters-in-law. Covered individuals would have to divest such interests within 30 days — either by selling them or placing them in a qualified blind trust — and the Attorney General could sue violators for civil penalties of up to twice the value of the interest or payment. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in either committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries are the public at large: the people who make federal law and execute it would no longer be able to hold personal financial stakes in foreign businesses or take money from them, and neither could their spouses, children, sons-in-law, or daughters-in-law. That would reduce the chance that a sitting official's personal or family wealth depends on a foreign government-linked business, and it would make any such tie a punishable violation rather than merely a disclosure line item. Honest officials with foreign holdings would also gain a clear rule, a blind-trust path to comply, and protection from suspicion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary people watching for foreign influence

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit the President, cabinet officials, and Members of Congress from holding any financial interest in, or receiving any payment from, a foreign business, closing a gap where such foreign ties are currently permitted so long as they are disclosed.

It would apply the same rule to the spouses, children, sons-in-law, and daughters-in-law of those officials, recognizing that foreign money can reach an officeholder through family members instead of the official's own account.

It would require divestiture within 30 days, either by converting the foreign interest to cash or other investments or by placing it in a qualified blind trust, and it would let the Attorney General sue violators for civil penalties of up to twice the value of the interest or payment.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on senior government officials and their immediate families who currently hold foreign financial interests or receive income from foreign businesses. They would have to sell those interests or place them in blind or diversified trusts within 30 days, and officials who knowingly violated the ban could face civil penalties of up to twice the value of the interest or payment. Foreign businesses that currently pay wages or dividends to U.S. officials' families would lose those payment channels.

drawbacks.text: The ban reaches the spouses, children, sons-in-law, and daughters-in-law of officials, including children 'of any age,' which would force divestiture by family members who neither sought nor hold public office and who may have built their own holdings before a relative entered politics.

The requirement to divest within 30 days of taking office or of regulations being issued could force rushed sales of complex family assets, potentially at a loss, and compliance for widespread small holdings (for example, foreign-exposed mutual funds) depends on how regulators define exceptions, since the text only exempts foreign companies publicly traded on U.S. exchanges.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost side is small and mostly falls on a tiny group: senior officials and their families who would have to sell foreign holdings or put them in trusts within 30 days, and public officials who hold diversified mutual funds with foreign exposure would need to structure that carefully, since the carve-out for publicly traded foreign companies may not cover every fund. The benefit is real but indirect: less personal financial exposure to foreign businesses at the very top of government. The larger problem is that the bill is overbroad in one respect — it reaches officials' spouses and children of any age, including independent adult children — which invites constitutional and fairness objections and may explain why the bill drew no cosponsors even as its underlying goal is widely shared.

outcome.mechanism: It went to two House committees the day it was introduced, neither ever considered it, and it expired with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Golden introduced the bill on September 24, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the Committee on Oversight and Reform and the Committee on House Administration.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action at any point in the two-year Congress.
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor in either party.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died without a vote, as all bills do when the Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senior government officials and their families who hold foreign financial interests are better off, because no restriction was ever enacted; the bill died without ever being debated.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration after it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one else signed on, so there is no record of where either party stood; the bill died with one sponsor and zero cosponsors.

industries.industry: Senior government officials and their families with foreign business ties
industries.note: The President, cabinet officials, Members of Congress, and their immediate families would lose the ability to hold foreign financial interests or receive payments from foreign businesses. Their loss is the point of the bill: it removes a channel through which foreign money can reach the people who write laws and execute them.
